title: Recovering From a Bad Decision
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece maps out a specific sequence for recovering credibility after a leader makes a bad call: first understand what caused the error, then articulate the lessons learned before going public, then involve the team in building a better process for next time. It argues that admitting fault only becomes credible once the leader can also explain what they'll do differently. The framing treats a bad decision not as something to apologize away but as raw material for organizational learning. It closes with the idea that a well-handled mistake can build more trust than it costs.
points: Recovery starts with working backward from the bad outcome to find the smaller decisions that caused it.
Leaders should articulate the lessons learned before admitting the decision was faulty to the team.
Involving the team in designing a better process builds appreciation for learning through failure.
A leader doesn't owe a full apology unless the decision harmed a specific group.
The article closes by calling the last bad decision the best teacher a leader can have.
quotes: Before acknowledging the bad call, good leaders attempt to understand what led to the choice and why it turned out so poorly.
Identifying the factors that produced the bad decision is the first step toward recovery.
A leader must be able to explain how they will avoid the same mistake next time before admitting to the larger team that the decision was faulty.
The more people who get the chance to work on the plan, the more the team will come to appreciate the power of learning through failure.
In the hands of a skillful leader, the best teacher is the last bad decision.
